chapter: Picnics, wagon advertising and saloon work
title: Seating and routine on the advertising wagon
summary: He describes how seven players sat on the wagon, the boys handing out bills, and playing only when the wagon stopped on corners.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: rent of furniture wagon, you see. Pretty big wagon. Yeah. Have low sides or would it have gates?
No, it had sides and it had a tailgate.
The top on it or was it out where you were sitting in the open?
No, some would have tops and some was open.
Do they look anything like these vegetable wagons you see today? Bigger? Or larger. Or larger. With the same shape?
Same shape.
What did you sit on there? Were the benches on the sides?
No, we had little falling chairs, little round seats, falling chairs.
When you sat there were you facing each other or were you playing? Oh yeah. Yeah, we were fair. How was the benches? That's all I'd like to know.
All right. There's a drummer. He was set right behind the driver. Yeah.
Facing the rear.
Yeah, facing. You know. Facing toward the back of the wagon.
Yeah, by the way.
And the trumpet would be opposite him. Trumpet and trombone side each other. Mm-hmm.
Facing each other. Yeah.
And on this side, well, clarinet would be on my left side, on the right side, with violin.
You'd be sitting along one side of the wagon and there on the other one on the other side? That's right.
And the trombone player, he'd be sitting in the rear with the bass violin player. See where he could use his slides.
Yeah, he'd be facing out the back of the wagon there. Yeah. Where would Charlie Moore be sitting?
Charlie Moore be sitting next to me.
Oh.
Right next to me. Right next to me, he'd be sitting in the bass violin player, right on this side, the drum one player on that side.
The bass, was the bass player looking towards, facing the drummer, is that right? The bass player?
Yeah, the bass player faced the drummer. From the other side?
Yeah, that's it. Yeah. Did you have the trombone next to him?
That's right.
What about other people on the wagon? Would the kids climb on like they do today? Oh, no, indeed.
No, indeed. That wagon was, really consists of about seven pieces.
You didn't have any dancers or singers or nobody like that?
No, no.
Just, and a driver maybe?
Maybe we'd have a fella up with the driver. He'd be hollering out, announcing out to the people, you know. And then, we'd have about three or four boys carrying dodges. Oh, man. You know what?
Carrying what? Notices, like, huh? Oh, yeah. Notices, yeah. Oh, yeah. Yeah.
Each one would have a bum like that. Were they walking around?
Yeah, they'd follow.
They'd follow.
I see. Hand them off to the crowd.

Yeah, you see, like, we'd stop on corners where it was business corners, like saloons. We'd stop, you know, and play. That crowd, and they could see what's going on. Now, sometime we'd ride, about two blocks or three blocks before we'd hit another solo. Well, them boys, they'd distribute bills all in residence. While you were moving from one to another.
Yeah. Would you play while you were moving from one place to another? Oh, no. Not play? No, we'd play right on the corner. You only played when the wagon stopped? Yeah, when the wagon stopped.
